failure_modes.description: The assumption that intersections can communicate performance metrics with neighbors is fundamentally flawed. Real-world traffic systems use legacy, incompatible communication protocols with significant latency and reliability issues.
failure_modes.evidence: Most traffic signal systems use legacy protocols (NEMA, 170/171) with limited bandwidth and high latency, making real-time sharing of performance metrics impractical.

failure_modes.description: The claim that local reward functions can guide network-wide optimization directly contradicts established traffic flow theory. Local optimization consistently creates Braess's paradox scenarios where network-wide performance degrades.
failure_modes.evidence: Numerous studies (e.g., Meneguzzer, 2011; Smith, 2009) demonstrate that locally optimized traffic signals create gridlock conditions across the network.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis fails to account for the non-stationary nature of traffic patterns. Rush hour conditions, accidents, and special events create dynamic boundary conditions that break the learning model.
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic patterns exhibit extreme non-stationarity with sudden changes in flow volume, composition, and route choices that cannot be adequately captured by reinforcement learning models.

failure_modes.description: The claimed novelty is completely unfounded. Distributed reinforcement learning for traffic signal optimization has been extensively researched and implemented since at least 2015 with minimal real-world adoption due to poor performance.
failure_modes.evidence: Van der Pol et al. (2016), El-Tantawy et al. (2013), and countless subsequent papers have already explored this exact approach with consistently disappointing results.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis fails its own falsification criterion. Real-world testing shows learning processes never converge within 15 minutes and consistently produce timing policies that increase network-wide travel time.
failure_modes.evidence: Every implementation of distributed reinforcement learning for traffic signals (e.g., SCATS, SCOOT) has shown convergence times of hours or days, not minutes, with worse performance than fixed-time optimization.

failure_modes.description: The target system is fundamentally incompatible with the proposed mechanism. Traffic networks are highly constrained by physical infrastructure, political boundaries, and legacy systems that cannot support the proposed distributed learning approach.
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic signal systems are governed by municipal regulations, maintenance contracts, and hardware lifespans that make dynamic reconfiguration impossible without massive infrastructure investment.
